An English instructor at the university shared an article on Instagram about the assassination attempt on Donald Trump, adding the comment: "If you're gonna shoot, man, don't miss." The post was re-shared by the "Libs of TikTok" account on X (formerly Twitter), and gained widespread attention.
A group of students, posting under a social media account called "CanesCritters," uploaded a video for a Digital Marketing class assignment in which a Black student is compared to a gorilla.

A professor in the Department of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies at the university, criticized the idea of free speech on campus, associating it with the rise of fascism, and mocked those who promote debate over resistance, saying the moral high ground is "for those who wish to drown in blood."
A student, in a private group chat, described the January 6 Capitol breach as "a peaceful occupation of the capitol and our people were provoked with tear gas and flash bangs!"

A part-time math instructor modified the state's mandatory Oath of Allegiance to align with her pacifist beliefs. The standard oath requires employees to "support and defend" the U.S. and California Constitutions "against all enemies, foreign and domestic." She inserted the word "nonviolently" before "support and defend," crossed out "swear," and circled "affirm." Previously, similar modifications had been accepted without issue during her employment with public schools.

An electrical engineering and computer science professor, author of a 1976 book called 'The Hoax of the Twentieth Century' which denies the systematic extermination of six million Jews during World War II, publicly endorsed Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's Holocaust denial statements, saying: "I congratulate him... It was about time an Islamic leader stated this publicly."

An emeritus professor of medicine publicly supported physician-assisted suicide and the removal of Terri Schiavo's feeding tube. (As context, Terri Schiava was a Florida woman who suffered severe brain damage in 1990 and was diagnosed as being in a persistent vegetative state. Her husband sought to have her feeding tube removed, arguing she would not have wanted to be kept alive in that condition; her parents fought to keep it in. The dispute went through years of court battles and became a national flashpoint in 2005, involving the Florida legislature, Governor Jeb Bush, Congress, and President George W. Bush, who signed emergency legislation aimed at keeping her alive. The feeding tube was ultimately removed and she died in March 2005.)

A student government denied Turning Point USA's application for campus recognition, citing the group's "misalignment" with university values, "confrontational language throughout the TPUSA website," the national organization's "Professor Watchlist," and the group's "actions of encouraging a growth in conflict rather than fostering communication."

A psychology professor posted on Facebook in response to Charlie Kirk's assassination: "Me thinks the word 'karma' is appropriate. Sad all the way around." In a second post, she wrote: "But when we tell y'all that statistically ... White American men are the most dangerous animals on the planet we're wrong. Let's not be hasty they say ..." She then deleted the posts.
A psychology professor, when asked during a social psychology class about her views on NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick's national anthem protests against police violence, said she "would kill him."
A student produced a "visual thesis" that focuses on Islamic extremism and criticized violence and bigotry against Israel.

A philosophy professor posted on Facebook: "I want the entire world to burn until the last cop is strangled with the intestines of the last capitalist, who is strangled in turn with the intestines of the last politician."

Nine students, including two student journalists, participated in an unapproved "die-in" protest on campus to object to what they saw as the university administration's failure to acknowledge faculty and staff safety concerns regarding its COVID-19 reopening plan.
A video circulated on Snapchat and Twitter showing an incoming student and two others laughing as one of them knelt on the chest of another who was saying "I can't breathe."

A math instructor wrote in a Facebook exchange that there were "no safe spaces in my classes" for students in the country illegally, and said he would report such students to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

A professor of industrial and systems engineering, public policy, and economics displayed a "Thin Blue Line" flag, commonly associated with the "Blue Lives Matter" movement, on his office door ("blue lives" refers to the lives of police officers). He said he aimed to present an alternative viewpoint and support law enforcement, asserting that "blue lives protect black lives."
A professor of politics and global studies posted tweets about a Las Vegas mass shooting suggesting that "white male entitlement" was a contributing factor to mass shootings.

A part-time anthropology lecturer was involved in a confrontation with members of the campus College Republicans during a counter-protest to a pro-Palestinian event. The College Republicans accused the lecturer of attempting to grab a student's sign and striking another student who intervened. The lecturer denied these allegations, asserting his commitment to nonviolence.

The School of Public Affairs invited Condoleezza Rice to speak on civil rights. Rice supported the war in Iraq, the use of torture on detainees, and helped implement other Bush administration policies.

Salman Rushdie, author of the 1988 novel The Satanic Verses, was invited by a college to deliver a commencement address. Rushdie had recently made comments equating pro-Palestinian campus protests to support for a "fascist terrorist group."
